title: Value-pool decomposition: how a dollar of chip revenue flows upstream to foundries, OSATs, EDA, IP, equipment and materials
why_it_matters: The money-flow map lists who pays whom but not how much. Sizing each edge (e.g. foundry revenue as a share of chip revenue, EDA+IP as a share of R&D spend, equipment as a share of capex) tells us where the money actually pools and is the base for every later economics unit.
questions: What were the 2025 (and 2019, 2023) revenue totals of each paid-for stage: chip sales, foundry, OSAT, EDA, design IP, wafer-fab equipment, test equipment, materials, distribution?
What share of chip-company revenue is paid out to each upstream stage, and how does this differ for fabless versus IDM firms?
Which edges double-count (e.g. foundry revenue is inside fabless COGS; IDM internal transfers never appear as market revenue)?
How much of the chip market is sold through distribution versus direct, and what gross margin does the channel take?
How did the split move between the 2023 trough and the 2025 peak?
subquestions: Foundry revenue / fabless+IDM outsourced wafer spend: which publisher sizes each (TrendForce, Gartner, company sums)?
EDA+IP market (ESD Alliance MSS) versus chip-industry R&D spend (SIA)
WFE (SEMI WWSEMS) versus chipmaker capex (company sums)
Materials (SEMI MMDS) split into fab vs packaging materials
Where is captive (IDM in-house) value invisible in market statistics?
primary_sources: WSTS Semiconductor Market Forecast and Blue Book (market totals)
SEMI Worldwide Semiconductor Equipment Market Statistics (WWSEMS) annual release
SEMI Materials Market Data Subscription (MMDS) annual materials-revenue press release

SIA State of the U.S. Semiconductor Industry (R&D and capex as % of sales)
Annual reports / 20-F of TSMC, UMC, ASE, Amkor, Synopsys, Cadence, Arm (segment revenue)

Yole Group packaging market press releases

title: IDM-to-foundry outsourcing flows: how much IDMs buy from foundries, from whom, and on what terms
why_it_matters: The IDM-to-foundry edge is evidenced as a relationship but its size and terms are unknown. Analog/MCU/automotive IDMs (and Intel for leading-edge tiles) increasingly outsource, which shifts capex risk onto foundries and changes who is exposed in a downturn.
questions: What share of wafers or COGS do major IDMs outsource to foundries (Intel, Infineon, NXP, STMicroelectronics, Renesas, TI, Microchip, onsemi, Sony)?
Which foundries serve them and at which nodes (TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries, Vanguard/VIS, Tower, SMIC, Hua Hong)?
What contract forms are used (LTAs, capacity reservation, joint-venture fabs such as ESMC, JASM, VSMC)?
How did IDMs' foundry commitments change during the 2021 shortage and the 2023-2024 correction (e.g. purchase-obligation disclosures)?
How does Intel pay TSMC for outsourced tiles and how is that shown in Intel Products vs Intel Foundry segment reporting?
subquestions: Purchase obligations / unconditional purchase commitments in IDM 10-K and annual-report notes
IDM 'fab-lite' strategy statements and outsourcing percentages in capital-markets-day presentations
JV structures: ownership, offtake rights and pricing between JV partners

title: Materials, wafer, gas and chemical supply contracts: pricing basis, LTAs, prepayments and qualification lock-in
why_it_matters: Fabs spend about US$73bn a year on materials, but the payment terms are unknown in the money-flow map. Wafer makers use LTAs with customer prepayments, gas suppliers use long on-site contracts, and qualification makes switching slow; this determines who carries price and supply risk.

How are specialty and bulk gases supplied (on-site plants, take-or-pay, contract length, pass-through of energy costs)?
How are photoresists, wet chemicals, CMP slurries and targets priced and contracted?
How long does qualification of a second-source material take, and who pays for it?
How did materials pricing and LTAs change through 2021-2025 (shortage, correction, neon/helium shocks, China gallium/germanium controls)?

why_it_matters: NVIDIA has multi-year cloud service agreements (US$27bn) with unknown purpose, and chip vendors have invested in their own customers. If chip demand is partly financed by the chip seller, reported demand overstates independent demand and risk sits with the vendor.

why_it_matters: The final revenue edge (OEM/cloud to chip company) is only evidenced as 'direct or via distributors'. How buyers pay (NRE for custom chips, prepayments to secure memory/HBM, LTAs from automakers) decides who carries inventory and capacity risk at the end of the chain.

why_it_matters: Chips reach devices through EMS/ODMs (Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron, Jabil, Flex) but whether the OEM or the EMS pays the chipmaker, and who holds the inventory, is not established. This matters for working capital, pricing power and where demand signals originate.

why_it_matters: Brokers are a recognised participant type but their economics are unknown. In the 2021 shortage open-market prices reached large multiples of list, and the grey market is also the main route for counterfeit parts, which drives defence and automotive sourcing rules.

why_it_matters: Chips cross borders many times before a device is sold, and profits are often booked where IP or procurement hubs sit (Singapore, Ireland, Switzerland, Netherlands) rather than where fabs are. This distorts country statistics and matters for tariffs and minimum-tax rules.

title: Die-cost economics: cost per transistor, die size, yield, mask sets and design cost across nodes
why_it_matters: Moore's-law economics (cheaper transistors each node) underpins the industry's business model. Evidence on whether cost per transistor still falls at 3nm/2nm, and how yield, die size and design/mask costs shape per-chip cost, decides who can afford the leading edge.

why_it_matters: SiC and GaN power chips were expected to grow with EVs, but overbuilt capacity, Chinese substrate price cuts and slower EV demand led to losses and restructuring (e.g. Wolfspeed's 2025 Chapter 11).
